title: U.S. Stripped of Measles-Free Status After 26 Years as Outbreaks Surge Nationwide
snippet: Declining vaccination rates and record-breaking case counts have led international health experts to determine that measles is once again endemic in the United States, erasing a historic public health achievement.
content:
WASHINGTON — In a devastating milestone for the nation's public health system, the United States has officially lost its status as a country that has eliminated measles, ending a 26-year stretch of triumph over one of the world's most contagious airborne diseases.

An independent panel of experts advising the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) determined that the U.S. no longer meets the criteria for measles elimination after a single viral strain was found to be continuously transmitting domestically for over a year. The decision, long feared by infectious disease specialists, follows sharp declines in routine childhood immunization rates and widespread outbreaks across multiple states.

A Predictable Public Health Crisis

Under international standards set by the World Health Organization and PAHO, a disease is considered endemic when the same chain of transmission persists within a country for 12 consecutive months or longer. Genetic sequencing conducted by public health laboratories, including a landmark study in Utah, confirmed that a single measles strain circulated uninterrupted from mid-2025 through mid-2026, accounting for hundreds of cases in that state alone.

Sustained transmission has also plagued communities in Pennsylvania, South Carolina, New York, and Wisconsin. Health officials have recorded more than 5,400 measles cases nationwide this year—the highest annual total since 1991. The vast majority of infections occurred among individuals who were either unvaccinated or had an unverified vaccination status.

Public health leaders point to rising non-medical school exemptions, growing vaccine skepticism, and political rhetoric questioning vaccine safety as the primary drivers behind the resurgence. Two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine provide 97% protection against infection, making the disease entirely preventable with adequate community coverage.

Severe Consequences for Vulnerable Populations

The return of endemic measles carries severe clinical risks. Roughly one out of every nine reported cases this year has required hospitalization, and at least 10 deaths have been confirmed nationwide. Beyond initial symptoms of high fever and severe rash, measles can cause 'immune amnesia,' stripping the body of its ability to fight off secondary infections like pneumonia. In rare instances, severe neurological damage can occur years later.

The shift also poses acute dangers for newborns too young for vaccination and individuals with compromised immune systems due to cancer treatments or organ transplants, who rely on high herd immunity to stay safe.

A Long Road to Recovery

The U.S. first declared measles eliminated in 2000, relying on high community vaccination rates to contain localized outbreaks sparked by international travelers. However, the erosion of public trust in recent years has dismantled those barriers.

The U.S. is not alone in its retreat; Canada lost its elimination designation last year, and Mexico currently faces a similar risk. Experts warn that regaining measles-free status will require a concerted, non-partisan effort to restore trust in routine immunizations and strengthen community-level public health infrastructure—a task that will prove far more difficult than losing the status in the first place.
